newsitem.title: USA: Gene linked to glaucoma discovered - researchers.
newsitem.headline: Gene linked to glaucoma discovered - researchers.

text.p: Researchers announced on Thursday they had identified a gene linked to glaucoma, which could lead to improved screening for the eye disease that is a leading cause of blindness.

Doctors from the University of Iowa College of Medicine said they had discovered a gene linked to primary open angle glaucoma, the most common form of glaucoma and the second leading cause of legal blindness in the United States.

"The discovery ... will make it possible to identify individuals at high risk for this form of glaucoma before significant visual loss has occurred and to direct them toward sight-saving therapy," the researchers wrote in an article to appear on Friday in the journal Science.

Mutations in the gene, called TIGR, cause the relatively rare but potentially devastating juvenile form of open angle glaucoma, the researchers found. It appears also to be responsible for about 3 percent of the adult cases, with other as-yet-unidentified genes contributing to the rest.

"This gene causes juvenile onset open angle glaucoma," Iowa's Dr. Val Sheffield said in a telephone interview. "It is one of the genes that causes adult onset but we found that there is not a single gene (for adults)."
Since glaucoma is found in up to 2 percent of people above age 40, 3 percent translates into "about 100,000 Americans wallking around with mutations in the TIGR gene," Sheffield said.

The researchers said the finding should within the foreseeable future lead to a gene test for people at risk. If people are monitored and diagnosed early, drugs and surgery can control the disease and preserve sight.
In the future, learning more about the gene's function could also lead to better therapies.
Co-author Dr. Ed Stone, also at Iowa, said the discovery may change the way doctors and patients think of glaucoma and other diseases that are common in people over 40.

"Historically, people have thought of those conditions as inevitable wear and tear, aging, cosmic rays, whatever," Stone told Reuters. "You don't have the feeling that it's an inherited thing. But we know it is.

"And one of the coolest things about this finding is that we're not talking about a gene that causes some relentlessly degenerative condition that we can't do anything about. We do have good treatments for glaucoma."

But glaucoma is a silent disease and irreversible damage to vision can occur before it is diagnosed. A fluid called aqueous humor inside the eye is blocked and gradually builds up pressure that damages the optic nerve.

The Iowa team in 1993 had narrowed their search for the gene to chromosome 1 by studying one large family in which the disease was prevalent. Working with researchers at six other institutions in the United States and Australia, they did additional studies and genetic linkage analysis that allowed them finally to pinpoint the TIGR gene.

They started with families with a known history of childhood glaucoma. Once they identified the gene, they began looking at a broader population of glaucoma patients in a clinic and found that about 3 percent of them had a mutation in the same gene, Sheffield said.
